title: Flannery O'Connor
hook: a Southern writer whose strange stories find grace in grotesque places

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman singing at the Lincoln Memorial, and a song asking for a hand. Your line was precious lord. Whose load did you carry a little of? Day nine hundred ninety-four.

A doctor's waiting room in the South. A respectable woman named Mrs. Turpin sits sizing everyone up: who's trashy, who's decent, who's beneath her. She's thanking Jesus, privately, that she was made the way she was. Across the room, a sullen college girl is glaring at her over a book. And then, without warning, the girl throws the book. It hits Mrs. Turpin in the face. The girl lunges at her, calls her an old wart hog and tells her to go back to hell. It's a scene from a short story called Revelation, and it's funny and awful at once. The writer was Flannery O'Connor. Today, a Catholic storyteller from Georgia.

Flannery O'Connor spent her later years on a family farm in Georgia, raising peacocks and living with lupus, the illness that had taken her father. She was a devout Catholic, and she wrote stories full of con men, killers, prophets, and very proper people who are much less proper than they think. Her characters are often ugly, violent or ridiculous. Readers have sometimes asked why a writer of faith would write such grim, odd stories. Her answer, put plainly in her letters and essays, was that grace often arrives as a shock, and that her characters were too sure of themselves to notice it any other way. So the book in Mrs. Turpin's face is not the end of the story. That evening, hosing down her pigs, she argues with God out loud. And then she sees something. A procession stretching up into the sky, a vast crowd on its way to heaven. At the front, the people she looked down on, singing and leaping. At the back, people like her, decent and orderly, still singing on key, but with shocked faces, their virtues being burned away. Jesus told the respectable leaders of his day something like this. In Matthew, in the King James Bible: "the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you." And Paul writes: "God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise." O'Connor's stories rarely end with anyone tidy. They end with someone struck, and seeing, maybe for the first time. Grace, in her fiction, doesn't knock politely. It throws the book.
screen: `A CATHOLIC WRITER ON A GEORGIA FARM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for grace in someone odd. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who gets under your skin. Not someone dangerous, just someone strange, loud, awkward, hard to like. A neighbor, a coworker, a relative at the holidays. Picture their face. Now look for one thing in them you missed. Something they carry. Something they do well. Something they might be hoping for. If you pray, you can hold them before God, just as they are. If you don't, simply let them be more than your first impression for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Flannery O'Connor. A Catholic writer from Georgia whose strange, often violent stories show grace breaking into the lives of people who are sure they don't need it.
Your line: grace in odd places. This week ran from a priest at a blackboard to a farm full of peacocks. Today, when someone strikes you as strange, look twice. Day nine hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: O'Connor's stories are read in classrooms, book groups and church study circles, where Christians talk about how grace can come through hard or strange moments.

fork.setup: you're Mrs. Turpin. a stranger has just thrown a book at you and called you an old wart hog and told you to go back to hell. that evening, alone with your pigs, what do you do?
options: forget it; she was clearly disturbed.
argue with God out loud about it.
call the girl's mother to complain.
fork.reveal: she argues with God, hosing down the pigs, and then sees a procession to heaven with the people she looked down on going first.

original.note: Greek: grace, an unearned gift — the word Paul uses for God's favor.

trapdoor: what you thought: dark Southern stories with no faith in them.
what it means: stories by a Catholic writer where grace breaks in through violence and embarrassment.
what a scholar hears: O'Connor's own explanation that her characters needed a shock to see; Revelation ends with the looked-down-on going first, as in Matthew 21:31.
